title: Mr. Downs' Student-to-Student MGCs
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. shares an example from colleague Mr. Gordon Downs, a Missouri 7th-grade social studies teacher, who extended the Moments of Genuine Connection strategy from teacher-to-student to student-to-student interactions. Downs structures brief interview breaks into class time — announced as 'My Break' rather than free social time — giving every student on the roster a chance to converse meaningfully with every classmate over the course of the year. The piece documents the social mechanics of how the practice unfolds, with students moving from friends to same-gender peers and finally across gender lines, and highlights four goals: eye contact, genuine listening, universal inclusion, and the possibility of new friendships. Stuart closes by noting that Downs completes this work in his final year before retirement, framing it as a model of purposeful professional culmination.
points: Extending the MGC framework to student-to-student interactions broadens its benefit: every student becomes a potential connector rather than only the teacher.
Structured micro-breaks — 'My Break' versus 'Your Break' — give teachers control over whether downtime is socially free or purposefully relational without disrupting class flow.
Predictable social patterns, with students gravitating first to friends and then to same-gender peers, can be anticipated and designed around so that all pairing combinations eventually occur.
A class roster used as a tracker ensures that no student reaches year-end without having had a meaningful one-on-one exchange with every classmate.
A teacher's final year of a career is no less an occasion for innovation and relational investment; Downs' example reframes career endings as opportunities for purposeful legacy-making.
quotes: He started it out like ice breakers for students to get to know each other and is attempting for every student to have several MGCs with each student in their class. I thought this was a cool way to help students understand the importance of valuing, respecting, and seeing their classmates.

I started having students interview classmates several years ago. I haven't been as consistent lately as I used to be. Typically, I give my students a small break (around 2 minutes) in the middle of the class period.

If I announce 'Your Break', they may talk about whatever, with whomever. If I announce 'My Break', they have to find someone that they have not interviewed yet and ask them 'pre-determined' questions.

When I taught 6th grade, it usually followed a predictable pattern. Students would start with interviewing their friends. Then the boys would interview other boys that they didn't know very well and girls would do the same.

Finally, boys would have to interview girls and vice versa. Those interviews were generally a little more awkward (and amusing) with the girls consistently taking the lead in the conversations while most boys would be looking down at their own feet.
